  • Byrd Theatre: the spring room (1928). The spring room (foundation, Tours): an underground spring breached in the 1927 excavation, and a retention pond of 30 by 30 feet, seen from a concrete opening past the boiler on the general manager's tour (Style Weekly, 2014; a 2019 travel piece gives a room 25 feet square). He says the water was never used for the air conditioning; a Byrd engineer on Cinema Treasures says its water can be pumped for it, and Wikipedia that it used to be. Its side of the stage and its depth are approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. [1]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The 1928 seats, by the American Seating Company, 19 inches wide: cast-iron end standards in a polychrome finish holding the aisle lights, maple scrolled armrests, and backs in a gold and crimson floral velvet (the curator, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn one to a row, near the cut; how many there were and where is approximate. [1] [2] [3]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025).   • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn one to a row, near the cut; how many there were and where is approximate. [1] [2] [3]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928).   • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928).   • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn one to a row, near the cut; how many there were and where is approximate. [1] [2] [3]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The 1928 seats, by the American Seating Company, 19 inches wide: cast-iron end standards in a polychrome finish holding the aisle lights, maple scrolled armrests, and backs in a gold and crimson floral velvet (the curator, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn one to a row, near the cut; how many there were and where is approximate. [1] [2] [3]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]

Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). A cast-iron "mushroom cap" air vent in the concrete floor under the seats: the way the cooled air from the three tunnels under the floor reached the house (foundation, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn one to a row, near the cut; how many there were and where is approximate. [1] [2] [3]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The orchestra floor, falling in rows toward the stage. The rows, their spacing and the rake are approximate; no seating chart was found. Cut down to the air tunnels' roof: the floor and the ground it is laid on. [1]

  • Byrd Theatre: stage (1928).   • Byrd Theatre: Wurlitzer organ (1928). The organ's rooms, on the fourth floor over the stage, forty-some steps up (Boomer, 2014): the general manager lists four, the blower room, the main and solo chambers and the relay room (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015), the foundation two pipe rooms over the center of the screen with the relays in a room of their own, the nomination three chambers. Drawn as four rooms side by side; the layout is approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). An opera-style box beside the stage, with a large mural behind it (nomination): a grand piano in one and a harp in the other, played from the organ console (nomination). The piano is in the left box and the harp in the right, as Rudisill (1986: "boxes to the left and right of the stage"), Richmond magazine (2021: the harp "in the right balcony") and a 2019 account (piano in the left alcove, harp and marimba in the right) agree; drawn so, house left and house right. The harp does not play: a marimba below it makes the harp's sound (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015; Mid-Atlantic Traveler, 2019). [1] [2]

The harp does not play: a marimba below it makes the harp's sound (Richmond Family Magazine, 2015; Mid-Atlantic Traveler, 2019). The marimba's place below the box is approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]

  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The balcony, an integral part of the theatre's visual effect (nomination); today 476 seats (Wikipedia). Its depth, rake and rows are approximate; the 1928 photograph shows its curved front, drawn straight. [1] [2]
  • Byrd Theatre: auditorium (1928). The 1928 seats, by the American Seating Company, 19 inches wide: cast-iron end standards in a polychrome finish holding the aisle lights, maple scrolled armrests, and backs in a gold and crimson floral velvet (the curator, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

The 1928 seats, by the American Seating Company, 19 inches wide: cast-iron end standards in a polychrome finish holding the aisle lights, maple scrolled armrests, and backs in a gold and crimson floral velvet (the curator, Curator's Corner, 2025). Drawn with a crimson seat and back, trimmed gold along the top; rows and aisles approximate. [1] [2] [3] [4]

  • Byrd Theatre: rooms (1928). The foundation's RFP lists, among the building's rooms, the general manager's office and restrooms off the main lobby, restrooms off the upper lobby, an office and vault, a rewind room, an electrical dimmer closet, and the attic. Where each lies is not given: placed approximately (the upper lobby's restrooms are not drawn). [1]

  • Byrd Theatre: the great chandelier (1928). The great chandelier in the dome: four thousand hand-cut crystals and three hundred bulbs in four colors, some two tons, lowered for cleaning and relamping (nomination). The foundation gives about 5,000 crystals, 500 bulbs, 2½ tons, 18 ft tall and 10 ft across; drawn 18 ft tall and 10 ft across. [1] [2]

The ground is today’s: cuts and fills since (the interstate, the floodwall) are in the elevation.

Camera how the camera works →

Looking north-northwest (bearing 328°), a fixed bearing with no snapping. Orthographic, tilted 33° down from the horizon: ground running into the picture is drawn at 0.55× its length and heights at 0.84×. 20 px per meter across the frame; the whole drawing is 1,608 × 940 px at 1:1.

Sources where the data comes from →

  • OpenStreetMap: 461 features read from the cached download, shared with region byrd-theatre.
  • USGS 3DEP elevation (United States (U.S. Geological Survey); bare-earth lidar, 1 m across most of the US, served by the National Map), fetched at 1 m per pixel and resampled to a 2 m grid. The ground runs from 66.5 m to 67.6 m above sea level (1.1 m of relief), drawn 1× taller than life. Buildings and bridges keep their true heights.

Ground what the ground is made of →

From the map, 1 mapped area of water, islands, parks, woods and other cover, and 38 ribbons of road, path, rail, canal and weir. Painted in 13 strips from back to front, 4 m deep each, so hills hide what is behind them (why). No contours.

Rivers and rapids how rapids are read →

No stretch of water read as rapids: places on a river where its surface, recovered from the lidar, falls faster than 4 m per km along its channel, measured over 200 m. Rock standing more than 1 m clear of the water around it is drawn as boulders; lakes, basins and the sea get neither. Both are inferred from the lidar, not observed.

Buildings where heights come from →

2 buildings, extruded from footprints of at least 12 m² that lie wholly inside the frame, from OpenStreetMap.

  • 0 (0%) from a height tag
  • 1 (50%) from the number of floors, at 3.4 m a floor
  • 1 (50%) guessed from the building’s type and size

Bridges how decks are placed →

No bridges in the frame.

Drawing paint order →

The winter palette, no dots, on a ground slab 0 m thick.
